title: Asking for Feedback on Yourself
meta: B2 · 约 280 词 · 场景：向他人要反馈

sections.heading: 1. Why "Any Feedback?" Gets Nothing
paragraphs: At the end of a one-on-one, you ask your engineer, "Any feedback for me?"
She smiles and says, "No, all good."
You both move on, and you learn nothing.
She is not lying.
The question is simply too broad, and the ==power== gap makes honesty risky.
Telling your manager what they do badly feels like a career gamble, so the safe answer wins every time.
**The more power you have, the less honest feedback you get by default.**
As a lead, this creates a dangerous ==blind spot==.
Your habits in meetings, your tone in code reviews, and your decisions under pressure all affect the team.
Yet you are the last person to hear about them, unless you __go looking for__ it ==deliberately==.
sections.heading_zh: 1. 为什么「有什么反馈吗？」问不出东西
paragraphs_zh: 1:1 快结束时，你问你的工程师：「对我有什么反馈吗？」
她笑笑说：「没有，都挺好的。」
你们俩就翻篇了，你什么也没了解到。
她没有撒谎。
只是这个问题太宽泛了，而且上下级之间的权力差距让说实话变得有风险。
告诉老板他哪里做得不好，感觉像是拿职业前途在赌，所以每次都是安全的回答胜出。
你的权力越大，默认情况下你听到的真话就越少。
作为 lead，这会造成一个危险的盲区。
你开会的习惯、你在 code review 里的语气、你在压力下做的决定，都会影响团队。
可你却是最后一个听说这些的人，除非你刻意去找。

sections.heading: 2. Make It Easy and Safe to Answer
paragraphs: Replace the broad question with a narrow one.
"What's one thing I could do differently in our sprint planning?" is much easier to answer.
Asking for one thing also signals that you expect something, so "all good" __no longer works__.
Give people time, too.
Send the question a day before the meeting, so they can think instead of ==improvise==.
Some will feel safer writing it down than saying it to your face.
When the feedback comes, your reaction decides whether you get more.
Do not explain, defend, or __correct the details__.
Just say, "Thank you, that's really ==useful==," and ask one follow-up question if you need clarity.
**If you argue with the first piece of feedback, it will be the last one you get.**
Finally, show that it mattered.
A few weeks later, tell them what you changed because of what they said.
That visible ==follow-through== is what turns one brave comment into a habit.
sections.heading_zh: 2. 让回答变得容易又安全
paragraphs_zh: 把宽泛的问题换成具体的问题。
「在 sprint 规划会上，有哪一件事是我可以换个做法的？」这就好回答多了。
只要一件事，也是在表明你期待听到点什么，所以「都挺好的」就不管用了。
也要给对方时间。
提前一天把问题发过去，这样他们可以想一想，而不是临场发挥。
有些人觉得写下来比当面说更安全。
反馈来了之后，你的反应决定了你以后还能不能听到更多。
别解释，别辩护，也别去纠正细节。
就说一句「谢谢，这很有用」，如果需要弄清楚，再追问一个问题。
如果你跟第一条反馈争起来，它就会是你收到的最后一条。
最后，让对方看到这条反馈起了作用。
几周之后，告诉他们你因为他们的话改了什么。
正是这种看得见的跟进，把一次鼓起勇气的发言变成了一种习惯。

gist.q: 为什么问 "Any feedback for me?" 什么也得不到？
gist.a: 问题太宽泛，加上权力差距让说真话有风险，安全的回答总会胜出；你权力越大，默认得到的真话越少。

gist.q: 怎样问才更容易得到真实反馈？
gist.a: 换成很窄的问题，比如「我在迭代规划会上可以改的一件事是什么」；提前一天发问题，让对方有时间想，也可以书面回答。

gist.q: 收到反馈后应该怎么做？
gist.a: 不解释、不辩护、不纠正细节，只说谢谢，必要时追问一句；几周后告诉对方你因此改了什么。

dictation: The more power you have, the less honest feedback you get by default.
Replace the broad question with a narrow one.

If you argue with the first piece of feedback, it will be the last one you get.

prompts.q: 你想知道自己在周会上主持得怎么样。用 30 秒向一位下属要反馈：问题要窄，让对方觉得说真话是安全的。
prompts.ref: Can I ask you for a favor? I'm trying to get better at running our weekly sync, and I suspect I talk too much. What's one thing I could do differently in that meeting? It doesn't have to be big, and you don't need to answer now. Feel free to think about it and send me a message tomorrow. I genuinely want to hear it.
prompts.ref_zh: 能请你帮个忙吗？我想把我们的周会开得更好，我怀疑我说得太多了。在那个会上，有哪一件事是我可以换个做法的？不用是什么大事，也不用现在就回答。你可以想一想，明天给我发个消息。我是真心想听。

prompts.q: 一位同事给了你一条有点刺耳的反馈：你在代码评审里的评论语气太硬。用 30 秒回应：不辩解，感谢，并问一个追问。
prompts.ref: Thank you, honestly. That's not easy to say to someone, and it's really useful to hear. I hadn't realized my comments came across that way. Could you point me to one or two reviews where it felt harsh, so I can see what I'm doing? I'll try to change it, and I'd appreciate it if you tell me in a month whether it's better.
prompts.ref_zh: 真的谢谢你。这种话不好跟人说，听到对我很有用。我之前没意识到我的评论给人的感觉是这样的。你能给我指一两个让你觉得说话很冲的 review 吗？这样我能看看自己是怎么做的。我会试着改，如果一个月后你能告诉我有没有好一点，我会很感激。

words.ex: The power gap means juniors rarely challenge the tech lead in public.
Monitoring for the batch jobs is a blind spot in our setup.
We deliberately kept the first version small to learn faster.
The demo broke, so he had to improvise with screenshots.
That comparison table was really useful for the decision.
Good postmortems need follow-through on the action items.
Skipping the canary stage is a gamble we don't need to take.
We need more clarity on who owns the alerting.
Moving the launch date signals that quality comes first.
